records.source: Καὶ ἐγένετο ἐν μιᾷ τῶν ἡμερῶν διδάσκοντος αὐτοῦ τὸν λαὸν ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ καὶ εὐαγγελιζομένου ἐπέστησαν οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς καὶ οἱ γραμματεῖς σὺν τοῖς πρεσβυτέροις, καὶ εἶπαν λέγοντες πρὸς αὐτόν· Εἰπὸν ἡμῖν ἐν ποίᾳ ἐξουσίᾳ ταῦτα ποιεῖς, ἢ τίς ἐστιν ὁ δούς σοι τὴν ἐξουσίαν ταύτην;
records.gloss: And it came to pass on one of the days, teaching him the people in the temple and proclaiming the good news, came up the chief priests and the scribes with the elders, \v 2 and they spoke saying to him, Tell us by what authority these things you do, or who is the [one] having given to you the authority this?
pieces: One day, as Jesus was teaching the people in the temple and telling them the good news, the chief priests and the scribes came up to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, together with the elders.
"Tell us," they said to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "what authority do {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have to do these things? Who is it that gave {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} this authority?"

L.1: And it happened on one of the days, as {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was teaching the people in the temple and proclaiming the good news, [that] the chief priests and the scribes with the elders came up,
L.2: and they spoke, saying to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Tell us by what authority {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are doing these things, or who is the one who gave {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} this authority?"

R.1: One day Jesus was teaching the people in the temple courts and telling them the good news. The chief priests and the teachers of the law came up to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, and the elders came with them.
R.2: They said to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Tell us what authority {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have to do these things. Who gave {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} this authority?"

decisions.choice: the chief priests, the scribes and the elders: the groups that made up the ruling council in Jerusalem
decisions.reason: The senior priests, the experts in the law and the leading laymen formed the council. Jesus had named these same three groups as the ones who would reject him (9:22), and they were already looking for a way to destroy him (19:47).

decisions.choice: authority: the right to act, given by someone with the power to give it
decisions.reason: Their second question shows what they mean: who gave him the right? Teachers were expected to have been trained and approved, and the temple was under the priests' control.

decisions.choice: these things: what Jesus has been doing in the temple
decisions.reason: He had entered the city as king, driven the traders out of the temple and taught there every day (19:37-48). The leaders ask by whose authority he does all this.

decisions.choice: proclaiming the good news: announcing God's saving rule
decisions.reason: The verb is the one Luke uses for Jesus' preaching of the kingdom of God (4:43; 8:1).

decisions.choice: Jesus
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Jesus at the start of a new section.

decisions.choice: the temple courts; the chief priests; the teachers of the law
alternatives: the temple; the chief priests; the scribes
decisions.reason: Readable says that Jesus taught in the courts around the temple, as at 19:47. As in 19:47: "scribes" today suggests people who copy documents, so Readable says what these men did.

records.heading: A question about authority

records.source: ἀποκριθεὶς δὲ εἶπεν πρὸς αὐτούς· Ἐρωτήσω ὑμᾶς κἀγὼ λόγον, καὶ εἴπατέ μοι·
records.gloss: Answering then he said to them, Will ask you I also a word, and tell me:
pieces: He answered them, "I too will ask you a question. Tell {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} this:

L.3: And answering, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to them, "I also will ask you a question, and you tell {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}:

R.3: Jesus answered, "I will ask you a question too. You answer {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}:

decisions.choice: a word: a question, one matter
decisions.reason: The common word for word here means one point or question, as the next sentence shows.

decisions.choice: I also will ask you: a real answer, not a way of escape
decisions.reason: Teachers often answered a question with a question. Jesus' question holds the answer to theirs: if John was sent by God, then so was the one John said was coming (3:16), and the leaders had refused John (7:30).

decisions.choice: the quotation opens here and closes at the end of 20:4
decisions.reason: Jesus' question follows in the next sentence.

records.source: Τὸ βάπτισμα Ἰωάννου ἐξ οὐρανοῦ ἦν ἢ ἐξ ἀνθρώπων;
records.gloss: The baptism of John from heaven was it or from men?
pieces: John's baptism: did it come from heaven, or from {{gender:people|men}}?"

L.4: The baptism of John, was it from heaven or from {{gender:people|men}}?"

R.4: When John baptized people, was it God who sent him to do it? Or was it only a human idea?"

decisions.choice: from heaven: from God
decisions.reason: Jews often said "heaven" instead of naming God, out of reverence (15:18, 21).

decisions.choice: the baptism of John: John's whole work of baptizing and calling people to repent
alternatives: only the act of baptizing in water
decisions.reason: John baptized people as a sign that they were turning back to God, and he announced one greater than himself (3:3, 16). The question is whether God sent him.

decisions.choice: from men: from human beings, a human idea
decisions.reason: The word is the general word for human beings, set against heaven, that is, God.

decisions.choice: {{gender:people|men}}
decisions.reason: The word means human beings in general (m3).

decisions.choice: was it God who sent him to do it? Or was it only a human idea?
alternatives: was it from heaven or from people?
decisions.reason: Readable explains what "from heaven" means (m1) and what the other choice would mean.

records.source: οἱ δὲ συνελογίσαντο πρὸς ἑαυτοὺς λέγοντες ὅτι Ἐὰν εἴπωμεν· Ἐξ οὐρανοῦ, ἐρεῖ· Διὰ τί οὐκ ἐπιστεύσατε αὐτῷ;
records.gloss: And they reasoned among themselves saying that, If we say, From heaven, he will say, Why not did you believe him?
pieces: They discussed it among themselves and said, "If we answer, 'From heaven,' {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will ask, 'Then why did you not believe him?'

L.5: And they reasoned among themselves, saying, "If we say, 'From heaven,' {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will say, 'Why did you not believe him?'

R.5: They talked about it among themselves. They said, "If we say, 'God sent him,' Jesus will ask us, 'Then why did you not believe John?'

decisions.choice: reasoned among themselves: talked it over together, weighing the possible answers
decisions.reason: The verb means to work something out together. They do not ask what is true, only which answer is safe. The tenants in the parable will reason among themselves in the same way (20:14).

decisions.choice: believe him: accept John's message as from God
decisions.reason: To believe John was to repent and to accept the one he said was coming. The Pharisees and experts in the law had refused his baptism (7:29-30).

decisions.choice: Jesus; John
decisions.reason: Readable names the two men, since "he" and "him" mean different people here.

decisions.choice: the quotation opens here and closes at the end of 20:6; what Jesus would say is in single quotation marks
decisions.reason: The leaders go on talking in the next sentence.

records.source: ἐὰν δὲ εἴπωμεν· Ἐξ ἀνθρώπων, ὁ λαὸς ἅπας καταλιθάσει ἡμᾶς, πεπεισμένος γάρ ἐστιν Ἰωάννην προφήτην εἶναι·
records.gloss: If but we say, From men, the people all will stone us, having been persuaded for it is John a prophet to be;
pieces: But if we answer, 'From {{gender:people|men}},' the whole crowd will stone us, because they are sure John was a prophet."

L.6: But if we say, 'From {{gender:people|men}},' all the people will stone us, for they are convinced that John was a prophet."

R.6: But if we say, 'It was only a human idea,' all the people will kill us by throwing stones at us. They are sure that John was a prophet."

decisions.choice: will stone us: will kill us by throwing stones
alternatives: will throw stones to frighten us
decisions.reason: Stoning was the law's punishment for blasphemy and false prophecy (Leviticus 24:14-16; Deuteronomy 13:1-10), and an angry crowd might stone someone without a trial (Acts 7:58; John 10:31). To call a prophet of God a fraud would anger the people.

decisions.choice: having been persuaded: they hold a settled conviction
decisions.reason: The perfect tense describes a conviction already formed and still held.

decisions.choice: all the people: the crowds listening in the temple
decisions.reason: As in 19:48 and 20:1, the people who hang on Jesus' words. The leaders fear them again in 20:19.

decisions.choice: {{gender:people|men}}
decisions.reason: As in 20:4: human beings in general.

decisions.choice: It was only a human idea; kill us by throwing stones at us
decisions.reason: Readable keeps the wording of its 20:4 and explains what stoning was (m1).

records.source: καὶ ἀπεκρίθησαν μὴ εἰδέναι πόθεν.
records.gloss: And they answered not to know from where.
pieces: So they answered that they did not know where it came from.

L.7: And they answered that they did not know where [it was] from.

R.7: So they answered that they did not know where John's baptism came from.

decisions.choice: they did not know: they chose not to say
decisions.reason: Luke has just shown their reasoning (20:5-6). Their answer protects them; it is not an honest judgment. Leaders who will not judge John's authority cannot ask about Jesus'.

decisions.choice: from where: where John's baptism came from
decisions.reason: The question was about John's baptism (20:4).

decisions.choice: John's baptism
decisions.reason: Readable says what "it" is (m2).

records.source: καὶ ὁ Ἰησοῦς εἶπεν αὐτοῖς· Οὐδὲ ἐγὼ λέγω ὑμῖν ἐν ποίᾳ ἐξουσίᾳ ταῦτα ποιῶ.
records.gloss: And the Jesus said to them, Neither I tell you by what authority these things I do.
pieces: Jesus said to them, "Then I am not going to tell you either by what authority I do these things."

L.8: And Jesus said to them, "Neither do I tell you by what authority I am doing these things."

R.8: So Jesus said, "Then I will not tell you where {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} authority to do these things comes from either."

decisions.choice: neither do I: as they would not answer, so he will not
decisions.reason: "Neither" matches their refusal. Jesus has kept his part of the bargain (20:3); they have not kept theirs.

decisions.choice: I do not tell you: Jesus leaves the answer in his question
alternatives: Jesus hides the source of his authority
decisions.reason: Anyone who accepted that God sent John could see who sent Jesus. The parable that follows answers the question in another way: he is the owner's son (20:13).

decisions.choice: where {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} authority comes from
decisions.reason: Readable rephrases the question as one about the source of his authority, which is what the leaders asked (20:2).

records.source: Ἤρξατο δὲ πρὸς τὸν λαὸν λέγειν τὴν παραβολὴν ταύτην· Ἄνθρωπος ἐφύτευσεν ἀμπελῶνα, καὶ ἐξέδετο αὐτὸν γεωργοῖς, καὶ ἀπεδήμησεν χρόνους ἱκανούς.
records.gloss: He began then to the people to speak the parable this: A man planted a vineyard, and leased it to farmers, and went abroad times long.
pieces: Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} told the people this parable: "A man planted a vineyard and let it out to tenants. Then he went abroad and stayed away a long while.

L.9: Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} began to tell the people this parable: "A man planted a vineyard and leased it to tenant farmers, and went abroad for a long time.

R.9: Then Jesus told the people this story: "A man planted a vineyard, a field where grapes grow. He rented it to some farmers, who would take care of it for him. Then he went away to another country for a long time.

decisions.choice: planted a vineyard: Isaiah's song of the vineyard, where the vineyard is Israel
alternatives: an ordinary farming story with no background
decisions.reason: In Isaiah 5:1-7 God plants a vineyard, cares for it, and finds only bad fruit; the vineyard is the house of Israel. Jesus' hearers in the temple would know the song. Here the trouble is not the vineyard but those put in charge of it.

decisions.choice: leased it to tenant farmers: they worked the land and paid the owner a share of the crop
decisions.reason: Owners who lived far away often let their land to tenants who paid rent in produce. The farmers here are tenants, not owners or day laborers.

decisions.choice: went abroad: left the country
decisions.reason: The verb means to go away from one's own country, as in 15:13 and 19:12.

decisions.choice: to the people: the parable is told to the crowd, with the leaders listening
decisions.reason: Luke says it is told to the people, but the leaders know it is about them (20:19).

decisions.choice: the quotation opens here and runs to the end of 20:16
alternatives: a new quotation for each part of the story
decisions.reason: The whole parable is Jesus' speech. What the people in the story say is in single quotation marks.

decisions.choice: tenant farmers (L); tenants (B); farmers, who would take care of it for him (R)
decisions.reason: The word means farmers, but here they farm land they do not own (m2). Literal and Balanced say so; Readable explains it.

decisions.choice: a field where grapes grow
decisions.reason: Readable says what a vineyard is.

records.heading: The tenant farmers and the owner's son

records.source: καὶ καιρῷ ἀπέστειλεν πρὸς τοὺς γεωργοὺς δοῦλον, ἵνα ἀπὸ τοῦ καρποῦ τοῦ ἀμπελῶνος δώσουσιν αὐτῷ· οἱ δὲ γεωργοὶ ἐξαπέστειλαν αὐτὸν δείραντες κενόν.
records.gloss: And at season he sent to the farmers a slave, so that from the fruit of the vineyard they will give to him; but the farmers sent away him having beaten empty.
pieces: When harvest time came, he sent a servant to the tenants to collect his share of the vineyard's crop. But the tenants beat him and sent him back with nothing.

L.10: And at the [harvest] season he sent a slave to the tenant farmers, so that they would give him [some] of the fruit of the vineyard; but the tenant farmers beat him and sent him away empty-handed.

R.10: When it was time to pick the grapes, the owner sent one of his servants to the farmers. The servant was to get the owner's share of the grapes. But the farmers beat the servant and sent him away with nothing.

decisions.choice: at the season: at harvest, when the owner's agreed share of the crop was due
alternatives: at a time the owner chose
decisions.reason: The word means the right or fitting time; for a vineyard, the time of harvest. The owner asks only for what the lease gave him, some of the fruit.

decisions.choice: a slave: in the story, a figure for the prophets God sent to Israel
alternatives: an ordinary detail of the story
decisions.reason: Scripture speaks of God's servants the prophets, sent again and again and rejected (Jeremiah 7:25-26; 2 Chronicles 36:15-16). Jesus has said the same of Jerusalem (11:47-51; 13:34).

decisions.choice: empty-handed: with nothing
decisions.reason: The word means empty. The slave brought back none of the fruit.

decisions.choice: servant
decisions.reason: "Servant" in Balanced and Readable, as the style guide has it; the meaning decision (m2) keeps that the person was owned, and Literal keeps "slave". The servant stands for the prophets, whom Scripture calls God's servants (m2).

decisions.choice: the owner (R); he (L, B)
decisions.reason: Readable calls the man who planted the vineyard "the owner" all through the story; Literal and Balanced call him "master" where the Greek has that word (20:13).

records.source: καὶ προσέθετο ἕτερον πέμψαι δοῦλον· οἱ δὲ κἀκεῖνον δείραντες καὶ ἀτιμάσαντες ἐξαπέστειλαν κενόν.
records.gloss: And he added another to send slave; but they also that one having beaten and having dishonored sent away empty.
pieces: So he sent a second servant, but they beat this one as well, insulted him, and sent him off with nothing.

L.11: And he went on to send another slave; but they beat that one too and treated [him] shamefully and sent [him] away empty-handed.

R.11: So the owner sent another servant. The farmers beat him too. They treated him shamefully and sent him away with nothing.

decisions.choice: he added to send: he sent again
alternatives: he sent an extra slave along with the first
decisions.reason: "He added" with another verb is a Hebrew way of saying that someone did a thing again, common in the Greek Old Testament (Genesis 4:2; 8:12).

decisions.choice: treated shamefully: insulted and humiliated
decisions.reason: The verb means to take away someone's honor. The tenants add disgrace to the beating.

decisions.choice: servant
decisions.reason: As in 20:10: "servant" in Balanced and Readable (style guide); Literal keeps "slave".

records.source: καὶ προσέθετο τρίτον πέμψαι· οἱ δὲ καὶ τοῦτον τραυματίσαντες ἐξέβαλον.
records.gloss: And he added a third to send; but they also this one having wounded threw out.
pieces: Then he sent a third, and they wounded this one and threw him out.

L.12: And he went on to send a third; but they wounded this one too and threw [him] out.

R.12: Then the owner sent a third servant. The farmers hurt him badly and threw him out of the vineyard.

decisions.choice: wounded and threw out: the violence grows with each slave
decisions.reason: The first is beaten, the second beaten and shamed, the third wounded and thrown out. The next one sent will be killed (20:15).

decisions.choice: a third servant; out of the vineyard
decisions.reason: Readable says who was sent and where he was thrown.

records.source: εἶπεν δὲ ὁ κύριος τοῦ ἀμπελῶνος· Τί ποιήσω;
records.gloss: Said then the master of the vineyard, What shall I do?
pieces: Then the master of the vineyard said, 'What am I to do?

L.13: Then the master of the vineyard said, 'What shall I do?

R.13: Then the owner of the vineyard said, 'What should I do?

decisions.choice: What shall I do?: the owner's patience
decisions.reason: Instead of punishing the tenants, the owner looks for one more way to reach them, as God sent prophet after prophet before judging (2 Chronicles 36:15-16).

decisions.choice: the master: the owner of the vineyard
decisions.reason: In the parable the word means the man who owns the vineyard, as "lord of the vineyard" in 20:15. He stands for God, but within the story he is a figure, not addressed as God.

decisions.choice: owner (R); master (L, B)
decisions.reason: As in 20:10: Readable says "owner"; Literal and Balanced keep "master", the Luke convention for this word in parables.

decisions.choice: the owner's words open here in single quotation marks and close at the end of 20:13
decisions.reason: His thoughts go on in the next sentence.

records.source: πέμψω τὸν υἱόν μου τὸν ἀγαπητόν· ἴσως τοῦτον ἐντραπήσονται.
records.gloss: I will send the son of me the beloved; perhaps this one they will respect.
pieces: I will send my son, the one I love. It may be that they will show him respect.'

L.13: I will send my beloved son; perhaps they will respect him.'

R.13: I will send my own dear son. Maybe they will treat him with respect.'

decisions.choice: my beloved son: the words God spoke of Jesus at his baptism
alternatives: only a father's affection in the story
decisions.reason: At the baptism the voice from heaven said, "You are my beloved son" (3:22). The hearers do not know that yet, but Luke's readers do: the son in the story stands for Jesus himself.

decisions.choice: respect: show regard, feel shame before
decisions.reason: The verb means to turn toward someone with respect (18:2, 4). The owner hopes they will honor his son as they would not honor his slaves.

decisions.choice: perhaps: the owner hopes for the best
decisions.reason: The word expresses a real possibility, not certainty.

decisions.choice: the one I love (B); my own dear son (R); my beloved son (L)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use everyday words for "beloved". Literal keeps the word that recalls 3:22.

decisions.choice: him (no deity_pronoun setting)
decisions.reason: The son is a figure in the parable, so the pronoun for him takes no setting, even though the figure points to Jesus.

records.source: ἰδόντες δὲ αὐτὸν οἱ γεωργοὶ διελογίζοντο πρὸς ἀλλήλους λέγοντες· Οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ κληρονόμος· ἀποκτείνωμεν αὐτόν, ἵνα ἡμῶν γένηται ἡ κληρονομία·
records.gloss: Having seen then him the farmers reasoned with one another saying, This is the heir; let us kill him, so that ours may become the inheritance;
pieces: But the tenants saw him coming and talked it over among themselves. 'This is the one who will inherit,' they said to each other. 'If we kill him, the property will be ours.'

L.14: But when the tenant farmers saw him, they reasoned with one another, saying, 'This is the heir; let us kill him, so that the inheritance may become ours.'

R.14: But when the farmers saw the son, they talked it over together. They said, 'This is the son who will one day own the vineyard. Let us kill him. Then the vineyard will belong to us!'

decisions.choice: the heir; the inheritance: the son who would receive the vineyard, and the vineyard itself
decisions.reason: The story does not explain how killing the heir would give them the land. Perhaps they think the owner far away or dead, and that land with no heir could be held by those who work it. The point is their greed and their contempt for the owner.

decisions.choice: let us kill him: Jesus foretells his own death at the hands of Israel's leaders
decisions.reason: Jesus has said that the chief priests, scribes and elders will reject him and that he will be killed (9:22; 18:31-33). The leaders listening understand that the story is about them (20:19).

decisions.choice: reasoned with one another: the same kind of talk as the leaders' in 20:5
decisions.reason: Luke uses similar words for the tenants and for the leaders who weighed their answer among themselves. The hearers can see themselves in the story.

decisions.choice: the one who will inherit; the property
decisions.reason: Balanced uses plain words for the legal terms.

decisions.choice: the son; who will one day own the vineyard
decisions.reason: Readable names the son and says what an heir is.

records.source: καὶ ἐκβαλόντες αὐτὸν ἔξω τοῦ ἀμπελῶνος ἀπέκτειναν.
records.gloss: And having thrown him outside the vineyard they killed.
pieces: So they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him.

L.15: And they threw him out of the vineyard and killed [him].

R.15: So they threw the son out of the vineyard and killed him.

decisions.choice: threw him out, then killed him: the order of the two acts
alternatives: killed him and then threw him out
decisions.reason: In Mark 12:8 the tenants kill the son and then throw him out. Matthew 21:39 and Luke have the order here. Some see in it Jesus' death outside the city (Hebrews 13:12), but the parable does not say so.

decisions.choice: the son
decisions.reason: Readable names the son.

records.source: τί οὖν ποιήσει αὐτοῖς ὁ κύριος τοῦ ἀμπελῶνος;
records.gloss: What therefore will do to them the master of the vineyard?
pieces: So what will the master of the vineyard do to them?

L.15: What, then, will the master of the vineyard do to them?

R.15: What do you think the owner of the vineyard will do to them?

decisions.choice: a question to the hearers, which Jesus answers himself
decisions.reason: Jesus asks the question and gives the answer in the next sentence, as in Mark 12:9.

decisions.choice: do you think
decisions.reason: Readable shows that Jesus is asking his hearers.

decisions.choice: the owner (R); the master (L, B)
decisions.reason: As in 20:13.

records.source: ἐλεύσεται καὶ ἀπολέσει τοὺς γεωργοὺς τούτους, καὶ δώσει τὸν ἀμπελῶνα ἄλλοις.
records.gloss: He will come and will destroy the farmers these, and will give the vineyard to others.
pieces: He will come and put these tenants to death, and give the vineyard to others."

L.16: He will come and destroy these tenant farmers and give the vineyard to others."

R.16: He will come and kill those farmers. Then he will give the vineyard to other people to take care of."

decisions.choice: to others: new people put in charge of God's people, in place of the leaders
alternatives: the Gentiles in place of Israel
decisions.reason: In the story the vineyard is not destroyed; the tenants are replaced. The leaders understand that they are the tenants (20:19). Jesus will give his apostles a share in ruling Israel (22:29-30). Some read "others" as the Gentiles.

decisions.choice: destroy: put to death
decisions.reason: The verb is used of killing (6:9; 17:27; 19:47). Jesus has also warned of the destruction of Jerusalem (19:43-44).

decisions.choice: the quotation that opened at 20:9 closes here
decisions.reason: Jesus answers his own question, and the parable ends.

decisions.choice: to take care of
decisions.reason: Readable says why the vineyard is given to others.

records.source: ἀκούσαντες δὲ εἶπαν· Μὴ γένοιτο.
records.gloss: Having heard then they said, Not may it be!
pieces: Hearing this, the people cried out, "May that never happen!"

L.16: And when they heard [this], they said, "May it never be!"

R.16: The people heard this and said, "No! That must never happen!"

decisions.choice: may it never be: a strong wish that something not happen
decisions.reason: The phrase is a strong refusal, used often by Paul (Romans 3:4, 6). The hearers recoil from what the story threatens.

decisions.choice: they: the people who heard the parable
decisions.reason: The parable was told to the people (20:9). They see that it speaks of judgment on Israel's leaders and of the vineyard given to others.

decisions.choice: the people
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say who answered (m2).

records.source: ὁ δὲ ἐμβλέψας αὐτοῖς εἶπεν· Τί οὖν ἐστιν τὸ γεγραμμένον τοῦτο· Λίθον ὃν ἀπεδοκίμασαν οἱ οἰκοδομοῦντες, οὗτος ἐγενήθη εἰς κεφαλὴν γωνίας;
records.gloss: But he having looked at them said, What then is the having been written this: [The] stone which rejected the [ones] building, this has become into head of corner?
pieces: Jesus looked straight at them and said, "Then what is the meaning of the words that are written, 'The stone the builders discarded has become the main stone at the corner'?

L.17: But {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} looked at them and said, "What then is this that is written: 'The stone which the builders rejected, this has become [the] head of [the] corner'?

R.17: Jesus looked at them and said, "Then what do these words in the Scriptures mean? 'The stone that the builders threw away has become the most important stone in the building.'

decisions.choice: Psalm 118:22: the rejected stone becomes the chief stone
decisions.reason: The words come from the psalm the crowd sang when Jesus entered the city (19:38, Psalm 118:26). The builders stand for Israel's leaders, who reject Jesus, and God gives him the chief place. Peter uses the verse in the same way (Acts 4:11; 1 Peter 2:7). The Greek follows the Greek Old Testament, which matches the Hebrew.

decisions.choice: head of the corner: the main stone at the corner of a building, which holds two walls together
alternatives: the capstone at the top of an arch or wall
decisions.reason: The phrase may mean the cornerstone laid at the foundation or the stone set at the top of a building. Either way it is the most important stone, the one the builders threw away.

decisions.choice: What then is this that is written?: if the hearers say it must never happen, what does Scripture mean?
decisions.reason: The people have just said "May it never be!" (20:16). Jesus answers that Scripture itself foretells the rejection of the stone and God's raising it up.

decisions.choice: looked at them: looked straight at them
decisions.reason: The verb means to look intently, as when the Lord looks at Peter (22:61).

decisions.choice: discarded; the main stone at the corner (B); threw away; the most important stone in the building (R)
alternatives: rejected; the head of the corner
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say in plain words what the image means (m2). Literal keeps the psalm's own phrase.

decisions.choice: Jesus' words open here and run to the end of 20:18; the psalm is in single quotation marks
decisions.reason: Jesus goes on speaking in the next sentence.

records.source: πᾶς ὁ πεσὼν ἐπ’ ἐκεῖνον τὸν λίθον συνθλασθήσεται· ἐφ’ ὃν δ’ ἂν πέσῃ, λικμήσει αὐτόν.
records.gloss: Everyone falling on that the stone will be broken; on whom but it may fall, it will crush him.
pieces: All who fall on that stone will be smashed, and if it falls on someone, it will grind {{gender:that person|him}} to dust."

L.18: Everyone who falls on that stone will be shattered; and on whomever it falls, it will crush {{gender:that person|him}} to powder."

R.18: Anyone who falls on that stone will be smashed. And if that stone falls on anyone, it will crush {{gender:them|him}} to dust."

decisions.choice: the stone that breaks and crushes: Isaiah 8:14-15 and Daniel 2:34-35, 44-45
alternatives: a new picture with no background
decisions.reason: Isaiah speaks of a stone over which many will stumble and fall and be broken. Daniel tells of a stone cut without hands that strikes the statue of the kingdoms and grinds it to chaff; it stands for the kingdom God sets up. Jesus joins the pictures: the rejected stone judges those who reject it.

decisions.choice: crush to powder: grind to dust
decisions.reason: The verb first meant to winnow, to toss grain so the wind blows away the chaff, and then to scatter or crush. In the Greek of Daniel 2:44 it describes the stone crushing the kingdoms, which suits the picture of a falling stone here.

decisions.choice: falls on that stone: whoever opposes Jesus is broken by him
decisions.reason: The stone is Jesus (20:17). Whether people fall against him or he falls on them in judgment, those who reject him are destroyed (2:34).

decisions.choice: {{gender:that person|him}} (L, B); {{gender:them|him}} (R)
decisions.reason: The saying speaks of anyone at all, man or woman.

decisions.choice: the quotation that opened at 20:17 closes here
decisions.reason: Jesus' words end with this saying.

records.source: καὶ ἐζήτησαν οἱ γραμματεῖς καὶ οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς ἐπιβαλεῖν ἐπ’ αὐτὸν τὰς χεῖρας ἐν αὐτῇ τῇ ὥρᾳ, καὶ ἐφοβήθησαν τὸν λαόν, ἔγνωσαν γὰρ ὅτι πρὸς αὐτοὺς εἶπεν τὴν παραβολὴν ταύτην.
records.gloss: And sought the scribes and the chief priests to lay on him the hands in same the hour, and they feared the people; they knew for that against them he spoke the parable this.
pieces: The scribes and the chief priests wanted to get their hands on {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} then and there, but they were afraid of the people. They understood that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} had aimed this parable at them.

L.19: And the scribes and the chief priests sought to lay [their] hands on {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} in that very hour, but they feared the people, for they knew that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} had told this parable against them.

R.19: The teachers of the law and the chief priests wanted to arrest Jesus right away. But they were afraid of what the people would do. They knew that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} had told the story about them, and that they were the wicked farmers.

decisions.choice: lay hands on: seize, arrest
decisions.reason: The phrase means to take someone into custody (21:12; 22:53).

decisions.choice: and they feared: but they feared
decisions.reason: The word "and" here sets their fear against what they wanted, so it has the force of "but".

decisions.choice: for they knew: the reason they wanted to seize him
decisions.reason: The clause explains why they wanted to arrest him at once: they saw that the parable was aimed at them. Their fear of the people held them back.

decisions.choice: the teachers of the law and the chief priests
alternatives: the scribes and the chief priests
decisions.reason: As in 19:47: "scribes" today suggests people who copy documents, so Readable says what these men did.

decisions.choice: and that they were the wicked farmers
decisions.reason: Readable says how the parable was against them.

records.source: Καὶ παρατηρήσαντες ἀπέστειλαν ἐγκαθέτους ὑποκρινομένους ἑαυτοὺς δικαίους εἶναι, ἵνα ἐπιλάβωνται αὐτοῦ λόγου, ὥστε παραδοῦναι αὐτὸν τῇ ἀρχῇ καὶ τῇ ἐξουσίᾳ τοῦ ἡγεμόνος.
records.gloss: And having watched closely they sent spies pretending themselves righteous to be, so that they might catch of him a word, so as to hand over him to the rule and to the authority of the governor.
pieces: They watched {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} closely and sent agents who played the part of honest, devout men. Their aim was to seize on some word of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} and use it to deliver {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} into the governor's power and jurisdiction.

L.20: And watching [{{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}] closely, they sent spies who pretended to be righteous, so that they might catch {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} in [some] word, so as to hand {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} over to the rule and the authority of the governor.

R.20: So the leaders watched Jesus closely. They sent some men to spy on {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. These men pretended to be good people who wanted to obey God. They hoped to catch Jesus saying something wrong. Then they could hand {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} over to the Roman governor, who had the power to punish {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: spies: men hired or sent in secret to trap someone
decisions.reason: The word means someone planted or sent in secret to act for others. The leaders do not come themselves this time.

decisions.choice: righteous: sincere, law-keeping people with an honest question
decisions.reason: They pretend to be devout Jews troubled by a question of the law (20:22), not agents looking for a charge.

decisions.choice: the governor: the Roman governor of Judea, Pontius Pilate
decisions.reason: Judea was ruled by a Roman governor (3:1), and only he could put someone to death (John 18:31). Jesus will be handed over to Pilate (23:1).

decisions.choice: catch him in a word: trap him by something he says
decisions.reason: The verb means to take hold of. They want a saying they can use against him (11:54).

decisions.choice: honest, devout men; the governor's power and jurisdiction
alternatives: righteous; the rule and the authority of the governor
decisions.reason: Balanced says what sort of righteousness they put on (m2) and puts the legal phrase in plain words.

decisions.choice: Roman; who had the power to punish him
decisions.reason: Readable says who the governor was and why they wanted him involved (m3).

records.heading: Paying tribute to Caesar

records.source: καὶ ἐπηρώτησαν αὐτὸν λέγοντες· Διδάσκαλε, οἴδαμεν ὅτι ὀρθῶς λέγεις καὶ διδάσκεις καὶ οὐ λαμβάνεις πρόσωπον, ἀλλ’ ἐπ’ ἀληθείας τὴν ὁδὸν τοῦ θεοῦ διδάσκεις·
records.gloss: And they asked him saying, Teacher, we know that rightly you speak and teach and not you receive face, but on truth the way of the God you teach;
pieces: So they put a question to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}: "Teacher, we are sure that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are correct in what {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} say and teach. No one's rank sways {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, and {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} teach the way of God with truth.

L.21: And they questioned {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, saying, "Teacher, we know that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} speak and teach rightly, and {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} do not receive [anyone's] face, but {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} teach the way of God in truth.

R.21: They asked {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Teacher, we know that everything {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} say and teach is right. You treat everyone the same, whether they are important or not. And {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} teach the truth about the way God wants people to live.

decisions.choice: you do not receive a face: you show no favoritism
alternatives: you do not accept anyone's appearance at face value
decisions.reason: To "receive the face" was a Hebrew way of saying to favor someone because of who they are (Leviticus 19:15; Galatians 2:6). The spies say Jesus is not swayed by rank or power, so he will not fear the emperor.

decisions.choice: the way of God: the life God requires
decisions.reason: "Way" is often used for how one lives, and "the way of God" for the life he asks of his people (Acts 18:25-26).

decisions.choice: we know: flattery meant to trap him
decisions.reason: What they say is true, but they say it to lead him into an answer that will condemn him (20:20, 23).

decisions.choice: No one's rank sways you (B); You treat everyone the same, whether they are important or not (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable explain the idiom (m1).

decisions.choice: the quotation opens here and closes at the end of 20:22
decisions.reason: The question itself comes in the next sentence.

records.source: ἔξεστιν ἡμᾶς Καίσαρι φόρον δοῦναι ἢ οὔ;
records.gloss: Is it lawful for us to Caesar tribute to give or not?
pieces: Does the law allow us to pay tribute to Caesar, or not?"

L.22: Is it lawful for us to give tribute to Caesar, or not?"

R.22: Does God's law allow us to pay taxes to Caesar, the Roman emperor? Or should we refuse?"

decisions.choice: tribute to Caesar: the tax paid to the Roman emperor by people under Roman rule
decisions.reason: Caesar was the title of the Roman emperor, at this time Tiberius (3:1). Since Judea came under a Roman governor in AD 6, its people paid a tax to Rome for each person. Judas the Galilean led a revolt against it (Acts 5:37), and many Jews hated it as a sign that a foreign ruler held God's land.

decisions.choice: lawful: allowed by the law of God
decisions.reason: The word is used for what God's law permits (6:2, 9; 14:3).

decisions.choice: the trap: either answer could ruin him
decisions.reason: If Jesus said "yes", he would lose the people, who hated the tax; if he said "no", he could be handed to the governor as a rebel (20:20; 23:2).

decisions.choice: the Roman emperor; Or should we refuse?
decisions.reason: Readable says who Caesar was (m1) and spells out the other choice.

records.source: κατανοήσας δὲ αὐτῶν τὴν πανουργίαν εἶπεν πρὸς αὐτούς·
records.gloss: Having perceived but of them the craftiness he said to them:
pieces: But {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} saw through their trickery and said to them,

L.23: But perceiving their craftiness, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to them,

R.23: But Jesus knew that they were trying to trick {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. He said to them,

decisions.choice: he said to them: the reading of the SBLGNT, with no question following
alternatives: he said to them, Why are you testing me?, the reading of many manuscripts
the same with "hypocrites" added, the reading of some manuscripts
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts add "Why are you testing me?", as in Matthew 22:18 and Mark 12:15. Several of the earliest manuscripts of Luke do not have it, and it may have come in from the other Gospels. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: craftiness: cunning, clever trickery
decisions.reason: The word is used of cunning that will stop at nothing (1 Corinthians 3:19; 2 Corinthians 4:2).

decisions.choice: they were trying to trick him
decisions.reason: Readable says what their craftiness was.

records.source: Δείξατέ μοι δηνάριον· τίνος ἔχει εἰκόνα καὶ ἐπιγραφήν;
records.gloss: Show me a denarius; of whom has it image and inscription?
pieces: "Let {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} see a denarius. Whose likeness and whose inscription does it carry?"

L.24: "Show {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} a denarius. Whose image and inscription does it have?"

R.24: "Show {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} a Roman silver coin. Whose picture and name are stamped on it?"

decisions.choice: a denarius: a Roman silver coin, the usual pay for a day's work, used to pay the tax
decisions.reason: The denarius was the coin of the empire (7:41; 10:35). The coins of Tiberius carried his head and words calling him son of the god Augustus. Jesus does not take out a coin himself; the questioners have one ready.

decisions.choice: image and inscription: the portrait of the ruler and the words around it
decisions.reason: A coin bore the face and name of the ruler who issued it, a mark of his ownership and authority.

decisions.choice: image: perhaps a reminder that people bear the image of God
decisions.reason: The same word is used in the Greek of Genesis 1:26-27. If the coin belongs to the one whose image it bears, people, made in God's image, belong to God (20:25). Jesus does not spell this out.

decisions.choice: denarius (L, B); a Roman silver coin (R)
decisions.reason: As in 10:35. The coin itself is the point here, with its picture and name, so no level gives a modern sum of money; the meaning decision gives its worth.

decisions.choice: likeness; inscription (B); picture and name stamped on it (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use words for what a coin shows.

records.source: ἀποκριθέντες δὲ εἶπαν· Καίσαρος.
records.gloss: And they said, Caesar's.
pieces: They answered, "Caesar's."

decisions.choice: Caesar's: the emperor's image and name
decisions.reason: The one-word answer refers to both the image and the inscription.

decisions.choice: The emperor's
decisions.reason: Readable reminds the reader who Caesar was.

records.source: ὁ δὲ εἶπεν πρὸς αὐτούς· Τοίνυν ἀπόδοτε τὰ Καίσαρος Καίσαρι καὶ τὰ τοῦ θεοῦ τῷ θεῷ.
records.gloss: He then said to them, Therefore give back the things of Caesar to Caesar and the things of the God to the God.
pieces: He said to them, "Then pay back to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God."

L.25: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to them, "Then give back the things of Caesar to Caesar, and the things of God to God."

R.25: Jesus told them, "Then give to Caesar what is owed to him, and give to God what is owed to God."

decisions.choice: give back: pay what is owed
decisions.reason: The verb means to give back or pay a debt. They asked whether to "give" the tax (20:22); Jesus says to give it back, as something already owed.

decisions.choice: the things of God to God: God's claim comes first and covers everything
alternatives: two equal realms, the state's and God's
decisions.reason: The coin bears Caesar's image and may go back to him. But God's claim is on the whole person (10:27). Jesus neither refuses the tax nor gives Caesar what is God's.

decisions.choice: then: it follows from the coin
decisions.reason: The word draws the conclusion from what they have just said: the coin is Caesar's.

records.source: καὶ οὐκ ἴσχυσαν ἐπιλαβέσθαι τοῦ ῥήματος ἐναντίον τοῦ λαοῦ, καὶ θαυμάσαντες ἐπὶ τῇ ἀποκρίσει αὐτοῦ ἐσίγησαν.
records.gloss: And not they were able to catch of the word before the people, and having marveled at the answer of him they were silent.
pieces: So with the people looking on, they found nothing in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} words to seize on. His answer left them amazed, and they had nothing more to say.

L.26: And they were not able to catch {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} in [{{deity_pronoun:his|His}}] word before the people, and marveling at {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} answer, they fell silent.

R.26: So they could not catch Jesus saying anything wrong in front of the people. They were amazed at {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} answer, and they kept quiet.

decisions.choice: before the people: in public
decisions.reason: They wanted a saying they could use against him in front of witnesses (20:20).

decisions.choice: marveling: amazed
decisions.reason: The verb is used for wonder at what Jesus says or does (4:22; 11:14). It does not mean they now believed him.

decisions.choice: with the people looking on, first
alternatives: before the people at the end
decisions.reason: Balanced puts the public setting first.

records.source: Προσελθόντες δέ τινες τῶν Σαδδουκαίων, οἱ ἀντιλέγοντες ἀνάστασιν μὴ εἶναι, ἐπηρώτησαν αὐτὸν λέγοντες· Διδάσκαλε, Μωϋσῆς ἔγραψεν ἡμῖν, ἐάν τινος ἀδελφὸς ἀποθάνῃ ἔχων γυναῖκα, καὶ οὗτος ἄτεκνος ᾖ, ἵνα λάβῃ ὁ ἀδελφὸς αὐτοῦ τὴν γυναῖκα καὶ ἐξαναστήσῃ σπέρμα τῷ ἀδελφῷ αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: Having come then some of the Sadducees, the [ones] denying a resurrection not to be, they asked him \v 28 saying, Teacher, Moses wrote to us, if of anyone a brother dies having a wife, and this one childless is, that should take the brother of him the wife and raise up seed to the brother of him.
pieces: Then some Sadducees came up, men who say there is no resurrection, and put a question to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}:
"Teacher, Moses gave us this law in writing: when someone's brother dies married but without children, the surviving brother is to marry the widow and raise children for the one who died.

L.27: Then some of the Sadducees came, those who deny that there is a resurrection, and they questioned {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}},
L.28: saying, "Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man's brother dies having a wife, and he is childless, his brother should take the wife and raise up offspring for his brother.

R.27: Then some Sadducees came to Jesus. The Sadducees were a group who said that the dead will never come back to life. They asked {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}},
R.28: "Teacher, Moses wrote a law for us. It says that if a man dies and leaves a wife but no children, his brother must marry her. That way the dead man can still have children to carry on his family.

decisions.choice: Sadducees: a party of leading priestly families who denied that the dead will rise
alternatives: a group of teachers like the Pharisees
decisions.reason: This is their only appearance in Luke's Gospel. They held power in the temple and gave the five books of Moses the highest authority. They said there was no resurrection, angel or spirit (Acts 4:1-2; 23:8). So they quote Moses.

decisions.choice: Moses wrote: the law of marriage to a brother's widow, Deuteronomy 25:5-6
alternatives: a custom not found in the law
decisions.reason: If a man died without a son, his brother was to marry the widow, and the first son would carry on the dead man's name, so that it would not be wiped out of Israel (Deuteronomy 25:5-6; compare Genesis 38:8; Ruth 4:5, 10).

decisions.choice: raise up seed: father children
decisions.reason: "Seed" means descendants. The children would count as the dead brother's.

decisions.choice: resurrection: the raising of the dead to life at the end of the age
alternatives: life of the soul after death
decisions.reason: The word means rising up, and here the bodily raising of the dead (14:14; Acts 23:6-8).

decisions.choice: The Sadducees were a group who said that the dead will never come back to life
alternatives: Sadducees, who deny there is a resurrection
decisions.reason: Readable explains who the Sadducees were in a sentence of its own.

decisions.choice: the quotation opens here and closes at the end of 20:33
alternatives: a new quotation in each sentence
decisions.reason: The Sadducees' case runs over several sentences.

records.heading: A question about the resurrection

records.source: ἑπτὰ οὖν ἀδελφοὶ ἦσαν· καὶ ὁ πρῶτος λαβὼν γυναῖκα ἀπέθανεν ἄτεκνος·
records.gloss: Seven therefore brothers there were; and the first having taken a wife died childless;
pieces: There were once seven brothers. The first married and died without having a child.

L.29: Now there were seven brothers; and the first took a wife and died childless.

R.29: There were seven brothers. The first brother got married, but he died without having any children.

decisions.choice: there were seven brothers: a case told as if it happened
decisions.reason: The story is meant to show that belief in the resurrection leads to nonsense. A Jewish story of the time, in the book of Tobit, tells of a woman who lost seven husbands (Tobit 3:8).

decisions.choice: took a wife: married
alternatives: took a woman into his house as a servant
decisions.reason: The usual way of saying that a man married.

records.source: καὶ ὁ δεύτερος καὶ ὁ τρίτος ἔλαβεν αὐτήν, ὡσαύτως δὲ καὶ οἱ ἑπτὰ οὐ κατέλιπον τέκνα καὶ ἀπέθανον·
records.gloss: and the second \v 31 and the third took her, likewise and also the seven not left children and died.
pieces: Then the second
and the third married her, and so on with all seven: each one died and left no children.

L.31: and the third took her; and likewise also the seven left no children and died.

R.30: Then the second brother married her,
R.31: and then the third. In the same way, all seven brothers married her and died, and none of them had children.

decisions.choice: and the second: the short reading of the SBLGNT
alternatives: and the second took the wife, and he died childless, the reading of many later manuscripts
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts fill out the verse so that it repeats what happened to the first brother. Several early manuscripts have the short form, which leaves the verb to be supplied from 20:31. The sense is the same. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the seven: all seven brothers in turn
decisions.reason: The second and third married her, and so did the rest; the seven together left no children.

decisions.choice: and so on with all seven: each one (B); all seven brothers married her (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say plainly that each brother married her in turn.

records.source: ὕστερον καὶ ἡ γυνὴ ἀπέθανεν.
records.gloss: Lastly also the woman died.
pieces: Last of all, the woman died too.

R.32: At last the woman died too.

decisions.choice: finally: last of all, after the seven
decisions.reason: The word means afterward, here at the end of the series.

records.source: ἡ γυνὴ οὖν ἐν τῇ ἀναστάσει τίνος αὐτῶν γίνεται γυνή;
records.gloss: The woman therefore in the resurrection of which of them becomes wife?
pieces: So when the dead rise, whose wife will she be?

L.33: So the woman, in the resurrection, whose wife of them does she become?

R.33: So when God raises the dead to life, which brother will she be married to?

decisions.choice: does she become: a present tense with a future sense
decisions.reason: The resurrection is still to come, so the question is about what will be.

decisions.choice: in the resurrection: they assume the life to come would be like this one
alternatives: they accept the resurrection for the sake of argument
decisions.reason: The Sadducees mean to show that the resurrection is absurd. Jesus answers that the life of the age to come is not like this life (20:35-36).

decisions.choice: when God raises the dead to life
decisions.reason: Readable says what the resurrection is.

records.source: οἱ γὰρ ἑπτὰ ἔσχον αὐτὴν γυναῖκα.
records.gloss: For the seven had her [as] wife.
pieces: All seven of them had her as a wife."

L.33: For the seven had her as wife."

R.33: All seven brothers were married to her!"

decisions.choice: for: the reason the question has no answer
decisions.reason: Each brother has the same claim, so the case seems to have no answer.

decisions.choice: the quotation that opened at 20:28 closes here
decisions.reason: The Sadducees' question ends here.

records.source: Καὶ εἶπεν αὐτοῖς ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Οἱ υἱοὶ τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου γαμοῦσιν καὶ γαμίσκονται, οἱ δὲ καταξιωθέντες τοῦ αἰῶνος ἐκείνου τυχεῖν καὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως τῆς ἐκ νεκρῶν οὔτε γαμοῦσιν οὔτε γαμίζονται·
records.gloss: And said to them the Jesus, The sons of the age this marry and are given in marriage, \v 35 but the [ones] having been counted worthy that age to obtain and of the resurrection the [one] from dead neither marry nor are given in marriage;
pieces: Jesus answered them, "In this age, men take wives and women are given to husbands.
But those who are judged worthy to have a share in the age to come and in the rising from the dead neither take wives nor are given to husbands.

L.34: And Jesus said to them, "The {{gender:children|sons}} of this age marry and are given in marriage,
L.35: but those who are counted worthy to attain to that age and to the resurrection from [the] dead neither marry nor are given in marriage.

R.34: Jesus said to them, "In this life, people get married.
R.35: But God will count some people worthy to live in the age that is coming. He will raise them from the dead. Those people will not get married.

decisions.choice: the sons of this age: the people of this present life
decisions.reason: "Sons of" means those who belong to something, as in 16:8. Here it simply means people living in this age, before the resurrection.

decisions.choice: marry and are given in marriage: men take wives, and women are given by their families
decisions.reason: A man married; a woman was given in marriage by her father (17:27). Together the verbs cover all marrying.

decisions.choice: counted worthy: by God
decisions.reason: The passive verb means that God judges them worthy, as Jews often spoke of God's acts without naming him (21:36).

decisions.choice: that age and the resurrection from the dead: the life of the age to come, entered by being raised
alternatives: life in heaven right after death
decisions.reason: Jews spoke of this age and the age to come (18:30). Jesus speaks of the resurrection of those who belong to God, "the resurrection of the righteous" (14:14).

decisions.choice: {{gender:children|sons}}
decisions.reason: The phrase means people of both sexes, as in 16:8.

decisions.choice: In this age, men take wives and women are given to husbands (B); In this life, people get married (R)
alternatives: The sons of this age marry and are given in marriage
decisions.reason: Balanced gives the idiom's meaning (m1) and shows the two verbs (m2); Readable says it in the simplest way.

decisions.choice: God will count some people worthy; He will raise them from the dead
alternatives: those counted worthy ... and the resurrection from the dead
decisions.reason: Readable names God as the one who judges them worthy (m3) and makes the resurrection a separate sentence.

decisions.choice: the quotation opens here and closes at the end of 20:38
decisions.reason: Jesus' answer runs over several sentences.

records.source: οὐδὲ γὰρ ἀποθανεῖν ἔτι δύνανται, ἰσάγγελοι γάρ εἰσιν καὶ υἱοί εἰσιν θεοῦ τῆς ἀναστάσεως υἱοὶ ὄντες.
records.gloss: neither for to die any longer are they able, equal-to-angels for they are, and sons they are of God of the resurrection sons being.
pieces: They will never die again, for they are equal to the angels; and having had their share in the resurrection, they are {{gender:children|sons}} of God.

L.36: For they cannot die anymore, for they are equal to angels, and they are {{gender:children|sons}} of God, being {{gender:children|sons}} of the resurrection.

R.36: They cannot die anymore. In this way they are like the angels. They are God's {{gender:children|sons}}, because God has raised them to new life.

decisions.choice: equal to angels: like the angels in not dying
decisions.reason: The word is found only here in the Bible. People raised to life share the angels' deathless life; they do not become angels. The Sadducees also denied that angels exist (Acts 23:8).

decisions.choice: for: why there is no marrying
decisions.reason: Marriage in this life carries on families in the face of death (20:28). Those who can no longer die have no need of it.

decisions.choice: sons of God, being sons of the resurrection: God's children, because they share in the resurrection
decisions.reason: "Son of" means one who belongs to or shares in something (16:8). Those raised by God are his children (6:35; Romans 8:23).

decisions.choice: {{gender:children|sons}}
decisions.reason: The phrase means men and women (m3).

decisions.choice: having had their share in the resurrection (B); because God has raised them to new life (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the meaning of the second "sons of" phrase (m3).

records.source: ὅτι δὲ ἐγείρονται οἱ νεκροὶ καὶ Μωϋσῆς ἐμήνυσεν ἐπὶ τῆς βάτου, ὡς λέγει κύριον τὸν θεὸν Ἀβραὰμ καὶ θεὸν Ἰσαὰκ καὶ θεὸν Ἰακώβ·
records.gloss: That but are raised the dead, even Moses showed at the bush, as he calls Lord the God of Abraham and God of Isaac and God of Jacob;
pieces: And that the dead are raised, even Moses made plain in the account of the burning bush, where he calls the Lord 'the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob.'

L.37: But that the dead are raised, even Moses showed in [the passage about] the bush, when he calls [the] Lord 'the God of Abraham and [the] God of Isaac and [the] God of Jacob.'

R.37: Even Moses showed that the dead will rise. In the story of the bush that was on fire, Moses calls the Lord 'the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.'

decisions.choice: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob: Exodus 3:6, from the bush that burned but was not consumed
decisions.reason: At the bush God told Moses that he was the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Exodus 3:6, 15-16). There "Lord" stands for the divine name, YHWH. The Sadducees appealed to Moses (20:28); Jesus answers from Moses too.

decisions.choice: at the bush: in the passage about the bush
decisions.reason: Before the Scriptures had chapter numbers, a passage was named by its subject (Mark 12:26; Romans 11:2).

decisions.choice: showed: made known, pointed out
decisions.reason: The verb means to reveal or report something (John 11:57; Acts 23:30). Moses' words point to the truth Jesus draws out of them.

decisions.choice: he calls: Moses, in what he wrote
decisions.reason: In Exodus God says these words. Jesus speaks of them as what Moses says, since Moses wrote them down.

decisions.choice: the account of the burning bush (B); the story of the bush that was on fire (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say that "the bush" means a passage of Scripture (m2) and which bush it was.

decisions.choice: the Lord
decisions.reason: The Greek has the ordinary word for Lord, so every level writes "Lord", and the meaning decision notes the divine name in the Hebrew.

records.source: θεὸς δὲ οὐκ ἔστιν νεκρῶν ἀλλὰ ζώντων, πάντες γὰρ αὐτῷ ζῶσιν.
records.gloss: God but not he is of dead but of living, all for to him live.
pieces: God is not a God of dead people but of living people, since all of them live in relation to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}."

L.38: Now {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} is not God of [the] dead but of [the] living, for all live to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}."

R.38: God is not the God of people who are dead. He is the God of people who are alive. All of them are alive to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}."

decisions.choice: not God of the dead but of the living: God's bond with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob outlasts death
alternatives: God has no concern for the dead
decisions.reason: God called himself their God long after they had died. He would not be God of people who no longer exist; they live to him, and he will raise them (13:28).

decisions.choice: all live to him: all who belong to him are alive in his sight
alternatives: all people owe their life to him
all will live for him in the future
decisions.reason: Death does not end their life toward God. A Jewish writing of the time says the same of the faithful martyrs, that they live to God (4 Maccabees 7:19; 16:25).

decisions.choice: God is not God of the dead: "God" is the predicate
alternatives: the God is not of the dead
decisions.reason: The noun without the article is what is said of him: he is not the God of the dead.

decisions.choice: Now he is not God of [the] dead
decisions.reason: Literal follows the Greek sentence, where "God" is what is said of the subject (m3); Balanced and Readable name God at the start.

decisions.choice: the quotation that opened at 20:34 closes here
decisions.reason: Jesus' answer ends here.

records.source: ἀποκριθέντες δέ τινες τῶν γραμματέων εἶπαν· Διδάσκαλε, καλῶς εἶπας·
records.gloss: Answering then some of the scribes said, Teacher, well you said;
pieces: Some of the scribes responded, "Teacher, that was a fine answer."

L.39: And some of the scribes answered and said, "Teacher, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have spoken well."

R.39: Some of the teachers of the law said, "Teacher, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} gave a good answer!"

decisions.choice: some of the scribes: experts in the law who believed in the resurrection
decisions.reason: Many scribes belonged to the Pharisees, who believed the dead would rise and disagreed with the Sadducees (Acts 23:6-9). They approve of Jesus' answer.

decisions.choice: the teachers of the law
decisions.reason: As in 19:47: "scribes" today suggests people who copy documents, so Readable says what these men did.

records.source: οὐκέτι γὰρ ἐτόλμων ἐπερωτᾶν αὐτὸν οὐδέν.
records.gloss: No longer for they dared to ask him anything.
pieces: From then on they did not dare put any more questions to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

L.40: For they no longer dared to ask {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} anything.

R.40: After this, they were afraid to ask {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} any more questions.

decisions.choice: for: the scribes' praise and the silence that follows go together
decisions.reason: Jesus' answers have ended the questioning. Luke's "for" links the scene's end with what came before.

decisions.choice: they: his questioners, all of them
decisions.reason: Chief priests, scribes, spies and Sadducees have all tried and failed (20:1-38).

records.source: Εἶπεν δὲ πρὸς αὐτούς· Πῶς λέγουσιν τὸν χριστὸν εἶναι Δαυὶδ υἱόν;
records.gloss: He said then to them, How do they say the Christ to be David's son?
pieces: Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to them, "How can people say that {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} is the son of David?

L.41: Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to them, "How do they say that the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} is David's son?

R.41: Then Jesus asked them, "Why do people say that {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} is King David's descendant?

decisions.choice: the Christ: the Messiah, God's anointed king
decisions.reason: With the article it is the title of the king God promised to send (2:11, 26; 9:20).

decisions.choice: David's son: the king promised from David's line
decisions.reason: God promised David that a son of his would reign forever (2 Samuel 7:12-16; Isaiah 11:1). "Son of David" was a title for the Messiah (18:38-39), and Luke has shown that Jesus is of David's line (1:32; 2:4).

decisions.choice: they say: people in general, as the scribes taught
decisions.reason: Mark 12:35 names the scribes. Jesus speaks to those around him about what was commonly taught.

decisions.choice: How do they say: Jesus does not deny that the Christ is David's son
alternatives: Jesus rejects the Messiah's descent from David
decisions.reason: Luke has already called Jesus David's son (1:32). The question shows that the title does not say everything: the Christ is also David's Lord (20:44).

decisions.choice: King David's descendant
decisions.reason: Readable says what "son" means here (m2).

decisions.choice: the quotation opens here and closes at the end of 20:44
decisions.reason: Jesus' question runs over three sentences.

records.heading: David's son and David's Lord

records.source: αὐτὸς γὰρ Δαυὶδ λέγει ἐν βίβλῳ ψαλμῶν· Εἶπεν κύριος τῷ κυρίῳ μου· Κάθου ἐκ δεξιῶν μου ἕως ἂν θῶ τοὺς ἐχθρούς σου ὑποπόδιον τῶν ποδῶν σου.
records.gloss: Himself for David says in book of Psalms, Said Lord to the Lord of me, Sit at right of me \v 43 until I put the enemies of you a footstool of the feet of you.
pieces: David himself says in the book of Psalms, 'The Lord said to my Lord: "Take {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} seat at {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} right hand
until I put {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} enemies under {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} feet as a footstool."'

L.42: For David himself says in [the] book of Psalms, 'The Lord said to my Lord, "Sit at {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} right hand
L.43: until I make {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} enemies a footstool for {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} feet."'

R.42: David himself wrote in the book of Psalms, 'The Lord God said to my Lord: "Sit here in the place of honor at {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} right side
R.43: until I defeat {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} enemies and put them under {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} feet."'

decisions.choice: Psalm 110:1: God speaks to the one David calls his lord
decisions.reason: In the Hebrew of the psalm the first "Lord" is the divine name, YHWH, and the second is a word for lord or master, used of a king. David hears God speak to someone David himself calls lord. Peter uses the verse of Jesus' being raised to God's right hand (Acts 2:34-35).

decisions.choice: at my right hand: the place of highest honor, sharing the king's rule
alternatives: a place on one side only
decisions.reason: To sit at a king's right hand was to rule with him. Jesus will say that the Son of Man will sit at the right hand of God's power (22:69).

decisions.choice: a footstool for your feet: enemies fully defeated
decisions.reason: A conqueror might put his foot on the neck of a defeated king (Joshua 10:24).

decisions.choice: David says in the book of Psalms: the psalm is headed as David's
decisions.reason: Psalm 110 is titled "Of David", and Jesus' argument rests on David being the speaker. Luke names the book of Psalms again in Acts 1:20.

decisions.choice: the Lord God; in the place of honor; defeat your enemies and put them under your feet
alternatives: the Lord; at my right hand; make your enemies a footstool
decisions.reason: Readable shows which Lord is which (m1), what the right hand means (m2) and what the footstool pictures (m3), as at Acts 2:34-35.

decisions.choice: the psalm in single quotation marks, and God's words within it in double marks
decisions.reason: Jesus quotes David, and David quotes God, so there are three levels of speech.

records.source: Δαυὶδ οὖν αὐτὸν κύριον καλεῖ, καὶ πῶς αὐτοῦ υἱός ἐστιν;
records.gloss: David therefore him Lord calls, and how of him son is he?
pieces: So if David calls {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} 'Lord,' how can {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} be David's son?"

L.44: So David calls {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} 'Lord'; and how is {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} his son?"

R.44: If David calls {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} 'my Lord,' then how can {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} be David's son?"

decisions.choice: how is he his son?: the Christ is more than David's son
alternatives: the Christ is not descended from David
decisions.reason: A father did not call his son "lord". If David calls the Christ his Lord, the Christ is greater than David. Luke has told how Jesus is both Son of David and Son of God (1:32-35); before the council Jesus will speak of sitting at God's right hand (22:69-70).

decisions.choice: him, he: the Christ
decisions.reason: The pronouns refer to the Christ of 20:41; "his" refers to David.

decisions.choice: David's son
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name David, since "his" could be misread.

decisions.choice: the quotation that opened at 20:41 closes here
decisions.reason: Jesus' question ends here.

records.source: Ἀκούοντος δὲ παντὸς τοῦ λαοῦ εἶπεν τοῖς μαθηταῖς·
records.gloss: Hearing then all the people he said to the disciples:
pieces: In the hearing of all the people, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to the disciples,

L.45: And while all the people were listening, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to the disciples,

R.45: All the people were listening when Jesus said to {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples,

decisions.choice: while all the people were listening: the warning is spoken to the disciples, but in public
alternatives: a private word to the disciples
decisions.reason: Jesus speaks to the disciples, but the crowd hears what he says about the scribes (compare 12:1).

decisions.choice: his disciples
decisions.reason: Readable names Jesus and calls the disciples his.

records.source: Προσέχετε ἀπὸ τῶν γραμματέων τῶν θελόντων περιπατεῖν ἐν στολαῖς καὶ φιλούντων ἀσπασμοὺς ἐν ταῖς ἀγοραῖς καὶ πρωτοκαθεδρίας ἐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς καὶ πρωτοκλισίας ἐν τοῖς δείπνοις, οἳ κατεσθίουσιν τὰς οἰκίας τῶν χηρῶν καὶ προφάσει μακρὰ προσεύχονται· οὗτοι λήμψονται περισσότερον κρίμα.
records.gloss: Beware of the scribes, the [ones] wanting to walk in long robes and loving greetings in the marketplaces and first seats in the synagogues and first couches at the dinners, \v 47 who devour the houses of the widows and for a pretext long pray; these will receive greater condemnation.
pieces: "Be on your guard against the scribes. They like to parade in long robes. They love it when people greet them in the marketplaces, and they love the front seats in the synagogues and the best couches at dinners.
They swallow up the property of widows, and they pray at great length to cover it up. These men will receive the heavier judgment."

L.46: "Beware of the scribes, who want to walk around in long robes and love greetings in the marketplaces and the first seats in the synagogues and the first couches at the banquets,
L.47: who devour the houses of widows and for a pretext pray at length; these will receive greater condemnation."

R.46: "Be careful of the teachers of the law. They like to walk around in long, fancy robes. They love it when people greet them with honor in the markets. They love to have the most important seats in the synagogues and at big dinners.
R.47: But they cheat widows and take their homes from them. Then they say long prayers so that people will think they are good. God will punish these men more than others."

decisions.choice: long robes: the long, flowing garments of men of rank and learning
decisions.reason: The word is used for a fine robe (15:22) or a festive garment. The scribes wear theirs to be noticed.

decisions.choice: greetings, first seats, first couches: public signs of honor
decisions.reason: Respected teachers were greeted with titles in the marketplace. The front seats in a synagogue faced the people (11:43), and at a dinner the couches nearest the host were the places of honor (14:7-11), since guests reclined to eat.

decisions.choice: devour the houses of widows: take widows' property
alternatives: eat in widows' homes as guests
decisions.reason: "House" here means a household's property. The scribes may have charged for advice, managed estates for their own gain, or pressed widows to give. Luke does not say how. The law and the prophets warned against wronging widows (Exodus 22:22; Deuteronomy 24:17; Isaiah 10:2), and the next scene shows a poor widow giving all she had (21:1-4).

decisions.choice: for a pretext: for show, to hide what they are
alternatives: as an excuse for being late
decisions.reason: The word means an outward show put on to cover the real purpose (Philippians 1:18).

decisions.choice: greater condemnation: a heavier sentence from God
decisions.reason: Those who know more and use religion to cover wrong will be judged more strictly (12:47-48).

decisions.choice: the teachers of the law
decisions.reason: As in 19:47: "scribes" today suggests people who copy documents, so Readable says what these men did.

decisions.choice: so that people will think they are good; God will punish
alternatives: for a pretext; these will receive condemnation
decisions.reason: Readable says what the pretext is for (m4) and who condemns them (m5).

decisions.choice: the best couches (B); the first couches (L)
decisions.reason: People reclined on couches at a formal meal (m2), so Balanced keeps the couch.
